This existing molecular held-out evaluation is distinct from the proposed descriptor-matched environment test at one fixed solute geometry: that test asks whether different solvent potentials with identical model descriptors can produce different electronic induction endpoints. It neither replaces nor negates Q's molecular evaluation.

Q_evaluation_quote:
EMLE Models Are Transferable and Accurate

Using the patched EMLE model with ϵ−1 = 0.6 from the previous sections, we evaluate
its performance, without further refinement, on a set of small, drug-like fragments that are
known to challenge MM and ME ML/MM approaches. These molecules, extracted from the
FreeSolv database, 27 exhibit chemistry similar to that of the training set shown in Figure 1B.
To ensure consistency, all simulation settings were retained from the previous calculations. In
addition to employing the MACE-OFF23(S) MLP, for which the effective dielectric constant
was tuned, we also tested the EMLE patched model in combination with MACE-OFF24(M)
and ANI-2x. The signed errors relative to experiment are presented in Figure 6.




                                              30
 Figure 6: Signed errors in HFE predictions relative to experiment for molecules
not included in the training dataset.        The models evaluated include MM FFs
(OpenFF/TIP3P), ME ML/MM models (MACE-OFF23(S)/MM, MACE-OFF24(M)/MM,
and ANI-2x/MM), and EE patched EMLE models (MACE-OFF23(S)/EMLE/MM, MACE-
OFF24(M)/EMLE/MM, and ANI-2x/EMLE/MM), scaled using an effective dielectric con-
stant of ϵ−1 = 0.6. The error bars denote the standard error of the MSE computed from
three replicates.


   Although the effective dielectric constant was optimized for MACE-OFF23(S) (RMSE
= 1.26 kcal/mol), both MACE-OFF24(M) (RMSE = 1.38 kcal/mol) and ANI-2x (RMSE
= 1.06 kcal/mol) demonstrate comparably good performance, indicating transferability of
the models to the test dataset. The largest discrepancies between the MACE and ANI-
2x models arise for polyhydroxy alkanes, where a critical interplay exists between intra-
and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. This stresses the importance of the underlying MLP
in determining simulation accuracy, particularly in capturing conformational preferences
such as hydroxyl group orientation, which directly affect HFE values. 26 For rigid molecules
(mobley_242480 and mobley_7378987), however, all EE models performs essentially equiv-
alently. Overall, the improvement achieved by the EE models over both OpenFF/TIP3P
(RMSE = 3.87 kcal/mol) and the ME ML/MM models (MACE-OFF23(S) RMSE = 3.91
kcal/mol, MACE-OFF24(M) RMSE = 3.77 kcal/mol, ANI-2x RMSE = 3.33 kcal/mol) is


                                            31
 substantial, underlining the importance of explicitly accounting for polarization.
   The MLP-agnostic nature of the EMLE models is expected, as no MLP-specific infor-
mation is used during training, i.e., only QM/MBIS and conformational data are provided.
This property supports transferability not only to chemically related molecules outside the
training set but also across different MLPs. Furthermore, the strong agreement with exper-
iment observed for both EE ANI-2x and EE MACE-OFF24(M) without reoptimizing the
dielectric constant suggests that the empirical scaling primarily compensates for deficiencies
in the MM/ML interactions (e.g., LJ terms) rather than errors in the MLP itself. Finally, we
note that the EMLE models developed here are unlikely to generalize to molecules that are
chemically very different from those in the training set. Developing a general EMLE model
trained on a larger, chemically diverse dataset, while incorporating the ideas presented in
this work, would therefore be a welcome next step.

abbreviation_Q_quotes:
Hybrid ML/MM approaches that combine machine learning (ML) potentials with

    molecular mechanics (MM) potentials offer a promising balance between computational

    cost and accuracy. Most ML/MM simulations reported to date employ mechanical

    embedding schemes, and rely on Lennard-Jones and Coulomb potentials to model in-

    termolecular interactions between the ML and MM regions. A promising approach to

    improving ML/MM schemes is to use electrostatic embedding, where polarization ef-

    fects on the ML region by the MM region are explicitly incorporated. The electrostatic

    machine learning embedding (EMLE) method has been developed for this purpose.

The idea behind QM/MM calculations is to model a small region of the system (typically
O ∼ 101 −102 atoms) using highly accurate but computationally expensive QM techniques,

                                                2
 while the remainder of the system is described using less accurate but computationally
inexpensive MM FFs. Current QM/MM studies mostly employ electrostatic embedding (EE)
strategies to describe the interactions between the QM and MM regions. In these approaches,
the MM point charge environment is explicitly included in the QM calculations, leading to
polarized wavefunctions or electronic density.
